title: Coasts & Beaches
keyIdea: A coast is the place where the land meets the sea; a beach is the part of the coast you can walk on. Coasts are not all the same: some are sandy, some are rocky and some are muddy. Each kind has its own plants and animals, such as lugworms and marram grass on sand, limpets and seaweed on rocks, and curlews and samphire on mud. Beach sand is rock and shell worn into tiny bits by waves over a very long time.
familyTip: Next time you see the sea, or a picture of it, play 'coast detective'. Ask: is the ground sand, rock or mud? What can you see living there? Look for squiggly lugworm piles on sand, limpets stuck on rocks, or birds with long beaks poking the mud.

visual.caption: Sandy or rocky? Drag each card, or tap it then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: trace the coast, look at sandy, rocky and muddy coasts, wear a rock into sand, and find each living thing its coast.

kid: A coast is where the land meets the sea. A beach is the part of the coast you can walk on. The edge of a pond or a lake is not a coast, because a coast needs the sea.
Coasts are not all the same. A sandy beach has soft sand for digging. A rocky coast has hard rocks and rock pools. A muddy coast has soft, sticky mud that your boots sink into.
Each coast has its own plants and animals. Lugworms dig in sand, and marram grass grows on sand dunes. Limpets and seaweed hold on to rocks. Curlews poke their long beaks into mud to find worms.
Where does sand come from? Waves crash on rocks again and again. Over a very long time, rocks and shells break into tiny bits. Those bits are sand.
adult: Ages 5 to 7. This fits the National Curriculum in England, Key Stage 1 geography, which lists coast, beach, cliff and sea as key physical features, and Year 2 science, living things and their habitats. Key words: coast, coastline, beach, shore, sandy, rocky, muddy, habitat, rock pool.

A coast is the strip where land meets the sea. Sandy beaches build up where waves drop sand; rocky shores and cliffs form where waves wear hard rock; mudflats and salt marshes form in sheltered places such as estuaries, where fine mud settles. Most beach sand is weathered rock, often quartz, mixed with broken shell, ground down over very long times.

Common mistakes: thinking every beach is sandy; calling the edge of a lake a coast; thinking sand grows or is made quickly; and thinking the same animals live on every coast. Limpets need a hard surface to clamp onto, lugworms need sand to burrow in, and curlews need soft mud to probe.

In the lab your child drags a finger along the coastline on a map, while taps on a lake or the open sea get a short correction. Next they drag a hand lens over sandy, rocky and muddy coasts. Then they crash waves on a rock until it wears from boulders to pebbles to sand. Last, they find a coast for six living things and sort six clue cards.

choices: the place where the land meets the sea
the edge of a pond or a lake
practice.hint: A coast always has two things side by side: land and the sea.
practice.explain: A coast is where the land meets the sea. The edge of a lake is not a coast, because a lake is not the sea.

practice.prompt: Which kind of coast has rock pools?
practice.hint: Rock pools are puddles of sea water left between hard rocks.
practice.explain: Rock pools form in hollows between rocks when the sea goes out, so you find them on rocky coasts.

practice.prompt: You find {a} shells on the sand and {b} more by the rocks. How many shells in all?
practice.hint: Put the two groups together: {a} and {b} more.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}. You found {=a+b} shells on the coast.

practice.prompt: {n} limpets cling to a rock. {k} more limpets clamp on next to them. How many limpets are on the rock now?
practice.hint: Start with {n} limpets and count on {k} more.
practice.explain: {n} + {k} = {=n+k}. Limpets clamp onto rocks so the waves cannot wash them away.

practice.prompt: Where does beach sand come from?
choices: rock and shells broken into tiny bits by waves
it grows on the sea floor
practice.hint: Think about waves crashing on rocks again and again for years.
practice.explain: Waves and weather slowly break rocks and shells into tiny bits. That takes a very long time.

choices: no, some coasts are rocky or muddy
pool.hint: Think about rock pools and sticky mud.
pool.explain: Coasts can be sandy, rocky or muddy. Each kind looks and feels different.

pool.prompt: Where would a curlew find its food?
choices: in soft mud, using its long beak
pool.hint: A curlew has a very long, curved beak.
pool.explain: Curlews poke their long beaks into soft mud to find worms and shellfish.

pool.prompt: Which lives on a rocky coast?
pool.hint: It needs something hard to clamp onto.
pool.explain: Limpets clamp onto rocks. Lugworms and marram grass need sand.

pool.prompt: Your boots sink into soft, sticky ground by the sea. What kind of coast is it?
pool.hint: Hard rock does not squish. What does?
pool.explain: Soft, sticky ground you sink into is mud, so it is a muddy coast.

pool.prompt: {n} curlews are on the mud. {k} more fly in. How many curlews now?
pool.explain: {n} + {k} = {=n+k} curlews poking the mud for worms.

pool.prompt: Tom says the edge of the village pond is a coast. Is he right?
choices: no, a coast is where land meets the sea
yes, any water edge is a coast
yes, if the pond is big
pool.hint: Is a pond part of the sea?
pool.explain: A pond or lake is water inside the land. Only the edge of the sea is a coast.

pool.prompt: What holds the sand together on a sand dune?
choices: the long roots of marram grass
pool.hint: It is a tall grass that grows on dunes.
pool.explain: Marram grass has long roots that hold the sand, which helps the dune stay in place.

pool.prompt: A rock pool has {a} crabs and {b} starfish. How many animals is that?
pool.hint: Add the crabs and the starfish: {a} and {b} more.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} animals in the rock pool on the rocky coast.
